Slide 2

Roadmap: the spacecraft half and the ground half of the same data loop

The lecture follows one loop of data. The SOC asks for observations, the MOC turns them into commands, a ground station sends them up, the spacecraft executes them, stores and protects its data, and sends them down at the next pass. The ground then processes, archives and distributes them.

The first half (Parts I–V) is the spacecraft side: formats, commands, security and getting stored data down. The second half (Parts VI–VIII) is the ground segment: stations, the processing chain, the MOC and the SOC, and real missions.

PART I

TT&C overview

Slides 4–8

Slide 4

Telemetry and command keep information flowing both ways between spacecraft and ground

Telemetry, command and data handling provide the two-way flow of information between the spacecraft and ground control: the downlink (transmission) and the uplink (reception), plus the management of payload data.

The design is driven by the mission, the orbit, the payload and the ground stations. The orbit matters most: a GEO satellite (Intelsat, Inmarsat) sees its ground station all the time, while a LEO spacecraft (Envisat, the ISS) sees a station only for minutes per orbit. It must therefore store data between contacts, or use a relay such as TDRSS in GEO.

Telemetry tells the ground how every subsystem is working, so faults can be detected and diagnosed; it may also carry the payload data. Commands let the ground change what the spacecraft does: reorient it, operate a mechanism, switch modes.

Check yourself
Why does a LEO Earth-observation satellite need a larger on-board memory than a GEO communications satellite?

Its ground contact is intermittent (minutes per ~100-min orbit), so data generated between passes must be stored until the next contact; a GEO satellite has a continuous link.

Slide 5

TT&C performs three functions — command, telemetry and tracking — often with a separate payload data linkfrom [2]

TT&C performs three functions: telecommand (Earth-to-space command bursts, kbps or even bps, highest reliability), telemetry (space-to-Earth status data, kbps to Mbps) and tracking (a ranging signal sent up, turned around by the transponder and sent back; the round-trip time gives distance and the Doppler shift gives radial velocity).

When the payload produces more data than the TM link can carry, a separate payload data transmission (PDT) link sends it at Mbps–Gbps to a payload ground station and payload data centre.

Try it in the deck: Click each link button to isolate TC, TM, ranging or payload data on the diagram.
Check yourself
Which TT&C link needs the highest reliability, and which the highest data rate?

Telecommand needs the highest reliability (a wrong or lost command can end the mission); the PDT link needs the highest data rate.

Slide 6

The TT&C and data-handling subsystem sits at the centre of spacecraft operations

The TM/TC and data-handling subsystem sits at the centre of the spacecraft (system context diagram): it connects the payload, AOCS/propulsion, power, thermal, deployment mechanisms and the command and data links, and through them the ground command centre and data-collection centre.

Commands, typically received on an S-band link, are decoded, queued and distributed; telemetry from each stage confirms execution. Low-demand functions (deployment) and high-demand ones (instruments) coexist, and high-rate payload data may use a separate X- or Ka-band downlink.

The spacecraft operates in modes, from a basic safe mode (kept alive from a command, thermal and power point of view) up to full platform and payload operation.

Check yourself
What does "safe mode" guarantee?

That the spacecraft stays commandable, thermally safe and power-positive, with the payload off, until the ground can intervene.

Slide 7

A basic TT&C subsystem is built for coverage and redundancy; the PDT subsystem is built for ratefrom [2]

A basic TT&C subsystem [2] has two low-gain antennas (LGAs) with opposite circular polarizations (LHCP, RHCP), a 90° hybrid, two diplexers, two receivers and two transmitters. The two LGAs give almost omni-directional coverage, so the spacecraft can be commanded in any attitude. Receivers are in hot redundancy (both always ON); transmitters in cold redundancy (one ON, the other switched in by command).

A transmitter, receiver and ranging turn-around are usually one unit: the transponder. The diplexer separates the TC and TM frequencies.

The PDT subsystem uses a switch (not a hybrid, which would lose 3 dB) and a medium- or high-gain antenna, because high data rates need every dB of EIRP.

Check yourself
Why accept the 3 dB loss of a hybrid in the TT&C chain?

Because coverage and fault tolerance come first: the hybrid lets either transmitter drive both antennas and either antenna reach both receivers.

Slide 8

Radio reminder: what you need from the communications lecture

This lecture takes the radio link as given. From the Communication Systems lecture you need four things. Bands: S-band for TT&C; X-band and K/Ka-band for payload data. Modulation: phase modulation with a residual carrier for commands and low-rate telemetry; suppressed-carrier schemes (QPSK, GMSK, 8PSK) for high rates.

Link budget: the received P/N₀ must exceed Eb/N₀ + 10 log Rb with about 3 dB margin. Tracking: ranging and coherent Doppler measured through the transponder; the flight dynamics team on the ground uses them to determine the orbit.

PRX/N₀ = EIRP + G/T − L − α + 228.6 [dBHz]
(P/N₀)req = Eb/N₀ + 10 log₁₀ Rb
Check yourself
By how many dB does the margin drop if the data rate doubles?

About 3 dB, because the required P/N₀ grows by 10 log₁₀ 2.

PART II

Telemetry data formatting

Slides 10–17

Slide 10

Telemetry data fall into three classes with very different rates

Housekeeping data monitor health and status (temperatures, pressures, voltages, currents, mechanism status). There may be thousands of parameters, but sampled only every 30 s to 2 min, so the rate is low.

Attitude data come from Sun/Earth sensors, star trackers, gyros and accelerometers; during transfers they may be sampled up to 4 times per second.

Payload data vary hugely; science and EO missions generate Mbit/s–Gbit/s and may need a separate high-rate system (as on Envisat) and compression. Deep-space images can take hours or days to send.

Check yourself
Estimate the bit rate of 1000 housekeeping parameters of 8 bits sampled every 30 s.

8000 bits / 30 s ≈ 270 bps.

Slide 11

Analogue telemetry is scaled, filtered, sampled and digitised

Analogue signals are first scaled to a common full-scale range (usually 0 to +5.12 V) at the source. A low-pass (anti-aliasing) filter removes components above half the sampling frequency; otherwise they appear as false lower frequencies. Analogue switches then sample the channels in turn, and an ADC (typically 8 bits) converts each sample.

Sampling is two-stage: a mainframe multiplexer for fast channels and a sub-multiplexer for slow channels sampled once or twice per minute, reducing complexity and harness mass.

Digital bi-level data (relay contacts) are set to logic levels, grouped into 8- or 16-bit words, serialised and merged into the PCM stream. Temperatures are measured with thermistors or thermocouples.

Nyquist: fs > 2 fmax
1 LSB = full scale / 2n = 5.12 V / 256 = 20 mV
Try it in the deck: Set the signal to 7 Hz and the sampler to 10 Hz: the ground sees 3 Hz.
Check yourself
A 7 Hz signal is sampled at 10 Hz. What frequency appears?

|7 − 10| = 3 Hz (aliasing).

Slide 12

Digital data enter the PCM bit stream, which is bi-phase modulated onto a sub-carrier

Digital serial data are stored in shift registers and inserted in 8- or 16-bit blocks. In PCM mode, ADC words, bi-level words and serial data are loaded into a parallel-to-serial converter and clocked out at the telemetry bit rate, with synchronization and identification codes inserted so the ground can find its way through the stream. The stream is bi-phase modulated onto a coherent sub-carrier.

In dwell mode the encoder samples one chosen channel repeatedly, by loading its address into the control and timing block — useful when investigating an anomaly.

Biphase-Mark has a transition at the start of every bit and an extra mid-bit transition for a "1", so the clock can always be recovered and there is no DC component.

Check yourself
Why does a telemetry stream need synchronization codes?

So the ground can find the start of each frame and assign every following word to the right channel.

Slide 13

A PCM message: 8 frames × 64 eight-bit words, with sync, frame ID and data channels

A simple PCM format has 8 frames of 64 eight-bit words. Words 1–2 hold a 16-bit sync code; word 3 is the frame identification; the rest are data channels.

A mainframe channel appears once per frame. A super-commutated channel appears several times per frame (higher rate). A sub-commutated channel shares one slot with others, appearing once every several frames (lower rate). This is typical for missions without a CCSDS packet system.

frame rate = bit rate / (words × 8)
mainframe rate = frame rate; super = k × frame rate; sub = frame rate / m
Try it in the deck: Change the bit rate and highlight each channel type.
Check yourself
At 4096 bps with 64-word frames, find the sample rates of a mainframe, a 4× super-commutated and a 1-in-8 sub-commutated channel.

Frame rate 4096/512 = 8 /s → mainframe 8 /s, super 32 /s, sub 1 /s.

Slide 14

Packet telemetry (CCSDS) replaced fixed PCM formats and improved interoperability

CCSDS packet telemetry (adopted by ESA through ECSS-E-ST-50) replaced fixed PCM formats. Application data are wrapped in source packets (header: source ID, sequence count, length); packets are grouped into virtual channels and fixed-length VCDUs; VCDUs are multiplexed into transfer frames. On the ground, frames are de-multiplexed and packets reassembled and routed from their headers. Each virtual channel can have its own rate, which saves bandwidth.

Check yourself
What is the advantage of packets over a fixed PCM frame?

Each source sends data when it has them, at its own rate, and the headers route them automatically — better efficiency and interoperability between agencies.

Slide 15

On the link, each TM frame becomes a CADU: sync marker, coding and randomizationfrom [2]

On the physical link a TM frame becomes a CADU (channel access data unit): an attached sync marker (ASM) + the frame + FEC bits (e.g. Reed–Solomon), optionally randomized (XOR with a pseudo-random sequence) so long runs of identical bits do not break bit synchronisation. Uncoded or RS-coded CADUs may then be convolutionally encoded — RS outside, convolutional inside = concatenated coding. With LDPC, frames are sliced into blocks, encoded and marked with a code sync marker.

Typical ESA choices: EO — RS or concatenated; near-Earth science — CC or concatenated; deep space — Turbo or LDPC.

Slide 16

Error-control coding: detect telemetry errors cheaply, correct them when the channel is noisy

Losing one telemetry frame is not catastrophic, so simple error detection is often enough. The frame is divided by a generator polynomial (x¹⁶ + x¹² + x⁵ + 1) and the remainder is sent; the ground divides again and flags a non-zero result. This detects but does not correct errors, and does not reduce the transmit power needed.

In noisy channels, convolutional coding (inner) is combined with Reed–Solomon (outer) to correct errors, including bursts. Deep-space probes such as Huygens use such coding to keep power and BER low over long distances.

Try it in the deck: Flip a random bit: the ground re-division gives a non-zero result.
Check yourself
Does adding a CRC improve the link budget?

No. It only detects errors; forward error correction is what lowers the required Eb/N₀.

Slide 17

Agencies standardise the codes: convolutional k = 7, r = 1/2 and Reed–Solomon (255, 223)

NASA/ESA guidelines standardise a convolutional code with constraint length k = 7 and rate 1/2, and the Reed–Solomon (255, 223) code: 223·I information bytes in, 32·I check bytes appended, with interleaving depth I = 1…5 (and 8). It corrects bursts of up to 16·I consecutive bytes; interleaving spreads a burst over I codewords.

RS rate = 223/255 ≈ 0.875 (any I)
correctable burst = 16·I bytes
Check yourself
With I = 5, how long a byte burst can be corrected?

16 × 5 = 80 bytes (640 bits).

PART III

Telecommand

Slides 19–24

Slide 19

Spacecraft commands range from simple pulses to digital words

Command types: low-level on–off (logic pulses to set/reset bistables); high-level on–off (12–28 V pulses for latching relays, ~90 mA, or RF switches, ~600 mA, with separate on and off coils); proportional (digital words for memory loads or register settings). ESA's Packet Utilization Standard (PUS) adds services such as memory loading, patching and telemetry.

Packet telecommand is layered: the application process layer is the human/computer interface; the system management layer translates commands into detailed form for packetization.

Slide 20

Packet telecommand is a seven-layer stack — click a layer

Packet TC layers, top to bottom: application process; system management; packetization (TC packets with a 48-bit header); segmentation (packets into virtual channels, 8-bit segment header); transfer (frames with 40-bit header and 16-bit error control); coding (CLTU: 16-bit start, n code blocks of up to 64 bits, tail; BCH (63,56) code, polynomial x⁷ + x⁶ + x² + 1); physical (RF link with four carrier modulation modes).

On board the layers run in reverse, and telemetry from each stage confirms receipt and execution.

Try it in the deck: Click each layer for its details.
Slide 21

A memory-load command frame protects every field by repetition and coding

In a memory-load command frame every field is protected: the spacecraft address and sync word selects the decoder; the mode word uses a 2-of-4 code so a single bit error gives an invalid word; each 12-bit word (8 data + 4 check bits) is sent twice — single errors are corrected, double errors detected, and one valid copy suffices. Philosophy: reject and resend rather than execute a wrong command.

Slide 22

Physical layer modes and TC error control: decode cheaply on board, retransmit when needed

The physical layer uses four carrier modulation modes: unmodulated carrier; modulated with an acquisition sequence; modulated with a CLTU; modulated with an idle sequence.

Encoding is cheap, decoding is expensive. For TM the decoder is on the ground; for TC it is on board, where electronics are constrained. CCSDS therefore chose a BCH code whose strength is detection — its failure even marks the end of a frame — combined with automatic retransmission (COP-1). Since 2021, LDPC codes are also allowed for TC [2].

Check yourself
Why is the TC code chosen for detection rather than strong correction?

Executing a corrupted command is dangerous, and a strong decoder is costly on board; detection plus retransmission (COP-1) gives safety cheaply.

Slide 23

CLTU and PLOP-2: how the TC receiver finds the start and end of each command unitfrom [2]

A TC frame is sliced into 56-bit blocks, randomized and BCH-encoded into 64-bit codewords; a CLTU adds the 16-bit start sequence 0xEB90 and a 64-bit tail. The PLOP-2 session: unmodulated carrier → 128-bit acquisition sequence (bit lock, E1: Inactive → Search) → start sequence found (E3: Search → Decode) → the tail is deliberately non-correctable (E4: back to Search) → idle sequence and next CLTU → carrier removed (E2: back to Inactive).

Try it in the deck: Step through the session and watch the receiver state.
Check yourself
How does the receiver know a CLTU has ended?

The tail sequence is a deliberately non-correctable codeword; the decoder reports an uncorrectable error and returns to Search.

Slide 24

PUS services are the shared vocabulary between spacecraft and ground

The Packet Utilization Standard (PUS, ECSS-E-ST-70-41C) gives every telemetry and telecommand packet a service type and subtype. For example, (3,25) is a housekeeping report and (1,7) reports that a command completed successfully.

Because the services are standard, the mission control system on the ground can process them with generic, reused software. Missions choose the services they need and may add private ones (types 128–255).

The services you will meet again: 1 request verification, 3 housekeeping, 5 event reporting, 9 time management, 11 time-based scheduling, 15 on-board storage and retrieval, 23 file management.

Check yourself
Which service tells the ground whether a command was executed?

Service 1, request verification (acceptance, start, progress and completion reports).

Which service is used to get stored data down?

Service 15, on-board storage and retrieval (packet store dumps).

PART IV

Securing the link

Slides 26–29

Slide 26

Space links face the same threats as any network — plus the cost of losing a spacecraft

A space link can be attacked like any network. Eavesdropping reads telemetry or payload data. Spoofing sends a fake command. Replay re-sends an old, genuine command recorded earlier. Jamming blocks the link. Ground intrusion attacks the control centre's networks — often the weakest point.

Each threat needs its own protection: encryption for confidentiality, a message authentication code (MAC) for authenticity and integrity, a sequence number for anti-replay. Jamming is an availability problem that cryptography cannot solve.

Check yourself
Why is the ground segment often the weakest link?

An attacker who controls the MOC can send commands that are perfectly authenticated; strong link cryptography does not help if the keys or consoles are compromised.

Slide 27

CCSDS SDLS adds a security header and trailer inside each transfer frame

The CCSDS Space Data Link Security protocol (SDLS) adds a security header after the frame header and a security trailer before the frame error check. The header carries the Security Parameter Index (SPI), an initialisation vector (IV) and a sequence number; the trailer carries the MAC.

A security association fixes the keys, algorithm and mode for one channel. Modes: authentication only, encryption only, or authenticated encryption (e.g. AES-GCM). Only the spacecraft and the MOC hold keys; the station and the network carry protected frames they cannot read.

Security costs bytes. With an 18-byte header and 16-byte MAC, a short telecommand pays a large relative overhead; a long telemetry frame hardly notices.

overhead = security bytes / (frame data + headers)
Try it in the deck: Switch the mode and move the frame size to see what is encrypted, what is authenticated and the overhead.
Check yourself
With 34 security bytes, what is the overhead for a 64-byte TC data field with 7 bytes of frame header and FECF?

34 / (64 + 7) ≈ 48 %.

Slide 28

Authentication and anti-replay: try to break into the spacecraft

A captured genuine frame still has a valid MAC, so authentication alone cannot recognise a replay. The sequence number solves this: the spacecraft remembers the last number it accepted and rejects any frame that is not newer (real SDLS uses an anti-replay window).

A forged frame or a frame with one flipped bit fails the MAC check and is discarded before anything is executed. Note what encryption alone does not do: it hides content but does not stop a replay.

Try it in the deck: Send two valid commands, then replay, forge and tamper — read the spacecraft's log.
Check yourself
An attacker records a valid "DUMP_STORE 2" command with SN 42 and replays it after SN 43 was accepted. What happens?

The MAC is valid but 42 ≤ 43, so the frame is rejected as a replay.

Slide 29

Keys, payload data encryption and the trade-offs of security

Keys live only in the spacecraft's cryptographic unit and a secure key-management facility. SDLS extended procedures cover over-the-air rekeying and security-association management. A key corrupted by radiation must be recoverable without creating a back door.

What is protected: command authentication is the baseline (NASA-STD-1006A requires protected command paths); telemetry is encrypted when it is sensitive; high-resolution payload data is often encrypted end to end.

Costs: overhead and latency, radiation-tolerant crypto hardware, key operations, and ground network security.

PART V

On-board data handling and getting data down

Slides 31–36

Slide 31

Classical OBDH: a central processor on a high-integrity serial bus

OBDH manages commands and data for TM and TC. Communications satellites handle user data; remote-sensing satellites handle large instrument volumes (SAR: 100 Mbps–1 Gbps). In the classical architecture a central processor connects to the RF subsystem and to AOCS, platform and payload over a high-integrity serial bus (ESA OBDH bus 250 kbps; MIL-STD-1553B). It decodes telecommands, is the central bus terminal, and may extract priority commands, fire pyrotechnics and execute time-tagged commands using ultra-stable oscillators.

Slide 32

On-board storage: real-time data now, playback data at the next pass

Between passes the spacecraft stores its data in a mass memory, sized for the longest gap between contacts plus margin. With PUS service 15, packets are routed into named packet stores; the ground commands a dump (playback) and, once receipt is confirmed, a delete.

Virtual channels keep traffic apart: e.g. VC0 for real-time housekeeping, VC1 for playback, VC2 and above for payload data. A circular store overwrites its oldest data when full (housekeeping); a bounded store stops recording (science that must not be lost).

Examples: Sentinel-2 carries 2.4 Tbit and dumps at 560 Mbit/s in X-band; JWST's 68 GB recorder fills in about a day of science and is emptied at up to 28 Mbit/s in Ka-band; Gaia sends about 40 GB/day at about 8.7 Mbit/s.

Check yourself
Why must the MOC check frame counters and packet sequence counts before commanding a delete?

A gap means data were lost on the way down; deleting would lose them for good, so the store is re-dumped first.

Slide 33

Anatomy of a pass: everything happens between AOS and LOS

A pass runs from AOS (acquisition of signal) to LOS (loss of signal). Typical order: acquire carrier and frame lock; check real-time housekeeping (is the spacecraft healthy?); uplink commands such as the schedule and dump commands, verified by service-1 reports; then dump stored data; ranging and Doppler run in the background.

Only the time left after acquisition and commanding is available for dumping, so the dump volume = rate × remaining time. Anything that does not fit waits for the next pass.

dump volume [GB] = R [Mbit/s] × tdump [s] / 8000
Try it in the deck: Change the pass length, commanding time and waiting volume until a backlog appears.
Check yourself
10-min pass, 1.5 min acquisition, 2 min commanding, 0.5 min margin, 300 Mbit/s. How much can be dumped?

6 min = 360 s × 300 Mbit/s / 8000 ≈ 13.5 GB.

Slide 34

Compression and storage: send less, keep it safe until the next pass

Compression removes redundant or unnecessary information. On-line (real-time) compression reduces rates 2–8×; off-line compression with a larger store achieves ~2× lossless and up to ~100× lossy. Standards include JPEG and CCSDS. Storage is solid-state, protected by error correction and scrubbing against SEUs, and organised in blocks or files — which drives the use of RTOS and remote file management (CFDP).

Slide 35

SCPS and CFDP: protocols for networks and files in space

SCPS (NASA with the US DoD) is a suite of network, security, transport and file protocols for satellite networks; adoption has been slow.

CFDP provides reliable file delivery: store-and-forward (no end-to-end path needed at one time), continuous delivery of unbounded streams, negative ARQ (only missing data are requested), proxy transfers, suspend/resume for predictable outages, garbage clearance against faults and SEUs, and remote file management.

Slide 36

Data downlinks: route, buffer, format, modulate, amplify — then fit it all into a few passes

Downlink data handling routes, buffers (FIFO or mass memory), formats, modulates (QPSK: 100 Mbps needs ~55 MHz) and amplifies (EIRP ~15 dBW with TWTA or SSPA and an antenna with some gain), within ITU/WARC flux limits. X-band (8025–8400 MHz) supports ~500 Mbps in LEO. Link-layer processing adds pseudo-randomization, differential encoding and FEC. LEO contact from high-latitude stations is only 3–10 minutes per ~100-minute orbit.

daily volume = R × passes × pass time / 8
Try it in the deck: Balance instrument rate, compression and passes so the downlink keeps up.
Check yourself
100 Mbps, 6 passes of 8 min per day: daily volume?

100×10⁶ × 6 × 480 / 8 = 36 GB/day.

PART VI

The ground segment

Slides 38–47

Slide 38

The ground segment: everything on Earth that is needed to fly the mission and use its data

The ground segment is everything on Earth needed to fly the mission and use its data: ground stations, the ground network that carries frames (SLE), the Mission Operations Centre (MOC), the Science/Payload Operations Centre (SOC), instrument teams and users, and simulators for testing and training.

The MOC flies the spacecraft; the SOC makes the science happen. Small missions often merge both in one control centre.

Try it in the deck: Click each element of the architecture.
Slide 39

Ground stations: antennas shared by many missions, booked weeks ahead

A ground station points its antenna using orbit predictions, transmits commands, receives and decodes telemetry frames, measures range and Doppler, time-stamps everything and forwards it to the MOC. Networks include ESA's ESTRACK, NASA's Deep Space Network (Goldstone, Madrid, Canberra) and commercial providers.

Stations are shared, so passes are scheduled; conflicts are resolved by priority, and deep-space antennas are booked weeks ahead (JWST: 12–20 weeks). A high-latitude station sees a polar LEO satellite on most of its ~14 orbits per day.

Check yourself
Why do many polar-orbiting missions use a station on Svalbard?

At high latitude the station sees the satellite on most orbits, giving many more passes per day than a mid-latitude station.

Slide 40

Space Link Extension: the standard "cable" between any station and any control centre

CCSDS Space Link Extension (SLE) services are the standard connection between any station (the provider) and any control centre (the user). RAF (Return All Frames) delivers every telemetry frame of a channel; RCF (Return Channel Frames) delivers the frames of one virtual channel; F-CLTU (Forward CLTU) sends commands to the station to radiate.

SLE allows cross-support between agencies and companies, and frames can be delivered online during the pass or retrieved later.

Check yourself
Which SLE service would the MOC use to send a command?

F-CLTU (Forward CLTU).

Slide 41

From radio signal to engineering values: the telemetry processing chain

At the station: demodulate, synchronise frames by finding the attached sync marker 0x1ACFFC1D, then derandomise and decode (Viterbi, Reed–Solomon, LDPC). Frames travel by SLE to the MOC.

In the MOC: frame checks (spacecraft ID, CRC, virtual-channel counter gaps) → SDLS check and decryption → virtual-channel demultiplexing → packet extraction (the first-header pointer shows where a packet starts; packets spanning frames are re-assembled) → routing by APID → decommutation into parameters → calibration → monitoring → archive, Level-0 production and forwarding of science to the SOC.

The chain is generic; the mission database defines every packet, parameter, calibration and limit.

Try it in the deck: Step through all 13 steps.
Check yourself
Why is a first-header pointer needed?

Packets have variable length and do not line up with fixed-length frames, so the receiver must be told where the first new packet in each frame begins.

Slide 42

Decode a real packet: header, service, parameters, calibration and limits

A CCSDS space packet starts with a 6-byte primary header: version (3 bits), type (TM/TC, 1 bit), secondary-header flag (1 bit), APID (11 bits), sequence flags (2 bits), sequence count (14 bits) and data length (16 bits, equal to the number of data-field bytes minus one).

The ground checks the length first: a mismatch means the packet cannot be trusted. The APID decides the routing; the PUS service/subtype tells what the data are; the mission database locates each parameter. Raw counts are calibrated into engineering units and checked against soft and hard limits.

data length field = data-field bytes − 1
example calibration: T = 0.01 · raw − 10 °C
Try it in the deck: Load the examples or edit the hex bytes yourself.
Check yourself
The first two header bytes are 08 64. What is the APID?

0x0864 = 0000 1000 0110 0100; the last 11 bits are 000 0110 0100 = 100.

A raw temperature reads 6200 counts. Calibrated value and status (soft 0…40 °C, hard −10…50 °C)?

0.01 × 6200 − 10 = 52 °C → hard-limit violation (alarm).

Slide 43

Monitoring turns thousands of parameters into a few alarms a controller can act on

Calibration converts raw counts to engineering units (polynomials, tables, or text states such as 0 → OFF). Limit checks use soft (warning) and hard (alarm) limits, often depending on context, e.g. eclipse or sunlight. Status consistency compares the reported state with the last command sent. Events (PUS 5) and on-board monitoring (PUS 12) report what the spacecraft noticed itself.

Anomaly handling: alarm and acknowledgement → contingency procedure → if needed safe the spacecraft and call the on-call engineer → anomaly report and investigation → recovery, validated on the simulator first. Autonomy buys time: Sentinel-2 can stay operational 72 hours after an on-board failure without the ground.

Slide 44

The telecommand chain: from a request to a verified action on board

Commands follow a controlled chain: request (SOC or MOC) → planning with constraint checks (power, thermal, pointing, data volume, passes) → command stack built from validated procedures, with range checks and a two-step arm/execute for critical commands → TC packets (often time-tagged, PUS 11) → SDLS authentication → FOP-1 numbering and retransmission → SLE F-CLTU to the station → on board, FARM-1 acceptance and execution → verification with PUS-1 reports, then a check of the effect in housekeeping.

Try it in the deck: Step through the chain.
Check yourself
A command shows an acceptance report but no completion report. How is it treated?

As not executed: the procedure stops and the team investigates before resending.

Slide 45

Time correlation: every packet is stamped with on-board time, but science needs UTC

Packets are stamped with on-board time (OBT), a free-running counter that drifts. The ground records the UTC earth-receive time of frames with known OBT, removes the light-time and known delays, and fits a correlation OBT → UTC. This is needed to date science data, determine the orbit and execute time-tagged commands correctly.

UTCevent = UTCreceipt − d/c − τon-board − τground
UTC(OBT) ≈ UTC₀ + (1 + δ)(OBT − OBT₀)
Check yourself
Light-time from 1.5 million km?

1.5×10⁹ m / 3×10⁸ m/s = 5 s.

Slide 46

Processing levels: from raw packets to science products

Processing levels (NASA Earthdata definitions): L0 — reconstructed, unprocessed instrument data at full resolution, with transmission artefacts removed; L1A — L0 time-tagged and annotated with ancillary data (calibration, geolocation); L1B — processed to sensor units; L2 — derived geophysical variables at the same resolution and location; L3 — variables mapped onto uniform space-time grids; L4 — model output or analyses of lower-level data.

Every level is archived; L0 is kept so products can be reprocessed when calibration improves. Timeliness classes range from near-real-time to reprocessing campaigns years later.

Try it in the deck: Click through L0 to L4 and their examples.
Check yourself
Why is Level-0 data kept forever?

Better calibration and algorithms come later; reprocessing from L0 produces improved products for the whole mission.

Slide 47

The ground segment is tested as hard as the spacecraft

The ground segment is a system with requirements and verification. An operational simulator runs the real on-board software to validate procedures and train the team. System validation tests command the real spacecraft from the real MOC before launch. A simulation campaign rehearses launch and early orbit with injected failures. An operational readiness review confirms that stations, networks, centres and people are ready.

PART VII

Mission and science operations centres

Slides 49–55

Slide 49

The Mission Operations Centre (MOC) is responsible for the spacecraft

The MOC operates the spacecraft as a vehicle: keeping it safe, healthy, in the right orbit and attitude, and executing the plan. Functions: monitoring and control, flight dynamics, mission planning, ground-station scheduling, on-board software maintenance, telemetry archive and distribution.

The flight control team includes the flight operations director, spacecraft operations manager, subsystem engineers, spacecraft controllers (SPACONs) and flight dynamics specialists. Example: ESA's ESOC in Darmstadt, which for Gaia plans and uploads, monitors health, determines and controls the orbit, and maintains the on-board software.

Slide 50

The Science Operations Centre (SOC) is responsible for the science

The SOC turns scientific goals into instrument operations and instrument data into calibrated, archived products. Functions: science planning and payload operation requests, proposal handling (observatories), instrument health and calibration, processing pipelines, archive and user support. Instrument teams (or instrument operations centres) calibrate their instruments and produce higher-level products with the SOC.

Example: ESAC near Madrid hosts the SOCs of many ESA science missions.

Check yourself
Name two SOC tasks that the MOC never does.

For example: evaluating observing proposals; producing calibrated science products; running the science archive and help desk.

Slide 51

MOC or SOC? Assign each task

The rule of thumb: anything about the vehicle (orbit, health, commanding, stations, on-board software) is MOC; anything about the science (proposals, requests, calibration, products, archive) is SOC.

The boundary is not universal: JWST's MOC and SOC are both at STScI; Hubble's flight operations are at NASA Goddard and its science operations at STScI.

Try it in the deck: Assign all ten tasks and check your score.
Slide 52

The planning loop: the SOC asks, the MOC checks and commands, the data come back

The SOC delivers its science plan and payload operation requests; the MOC merges them with platform activities, checks resources and constraints, generates the command timeline and uplinks it; the spacecraft executes; telemetry returns through the MOC to the SOC, whose results feed the next plan.

Planning runs at three horizons: long-term (months: mission phases, strategy, coverage), medium-term (weeks: requests and resource checks) and short-term (days: final, verified timeline). Gaia: the SOC generates the scanning law, science schedule and requests; the MOC uploads the planning products.

Slide 53

Flight dynamics: the MOC's navigators

Flight dynamics is the MOC's navigation team. It determines the orbit from ranging and Doppler (plus on-board GNSS in LEO, Delta-DOR in deep space), predicts passes and eclipses, plans manoeuvres, reconstructs the attitude, and screens conjunction warnings for collision avoidance. Its products go to the stations (pointing, AOS/LOS), planning (eclipses, passes) and control or the SOC (manoeuvres, attitude).

Slide 54

Mission control software: generic core, mission-specific database

A mission control system has a generic core and a mission-specific database. ESA's SCOS-2000 is used by Gaia, the Sentinels, BepiColombo, Solar Orbiter, Euclid and others; EGS-CC is its successor, first used by JUICE. Open-source options such as NASA's Open MCT (displays) and Yamcs (a full control framework) are popular with university and CubeSat teams.

Contents: the mission database, telemetry processing and displays, command stacks and procedures, archive, and interfaces to stations, flight dynamics, planning and the SOC.

Slide 55

Operations phases — and an illustrative day in the life of a LEO Earth-observation MOC

Operations phases: LEOP (launch and early orbit, 24/7, extra stations), commissioning (check-out and calibration), routine (highly automated, small team — about six engineers for Sentinel-2A and 2B), contingency (recovery from anomalies or safe mode) and end of life (disposal and passivation).

A routine day for a LEO Earth-observation MOC (illustrative): early S-band pass with health check and dump; orbit update from flight dynamics; daily meeting; X-band payload dumps; mission planning generates the next days' timeline; an afternoon pass uplinks and verifies it; unattended passes overnight with automatic paging of the on-call engineer.

Try it in the deck: Click the events on the 24-hour line.
PART VIII

Operations examples

Slides 57–64

Slide 57

Gaia: a classic ESA split — MOC at ESOC, SOC at ESAC, processing by a consortium

MOC at ESOC: mission planning and upload, receiving and distributing telemetry, health monitoring, orbit determination and control, on-board software. SOC at ESAC: scanning law and science schedule, payload operation requests, science-telemetry archive, calibration monitoring, feeding the Data Processing and Analysis Consortium (DPAC).

Link: three ESTRACK 35 m antennas (Malargüe, Cebreros, New Norcia), about 12.5 h/day of downlink in X-band at about 8.7 Mbit/s — about 40 GB/day compressed (about 100 GB raw).

Slide 58

Sentinel-2: flight operations at ESOC, a separate payload data ground segment

Flight operations at ESOC: a small dedicated team, S-band commanding and 2 Mbit/s housekeeping through Kiruna, a highly automated cycle (orbit maintenance → planning → downlink → performance monitoring), 15 days of stored commands and 72 h of autonomy after a failure.

Payload data ground segment: X-band stations at Matera, Maspalomas and Svalbard (560 Mbit/s), a laser link to the EDRS relay satellites in GEO, and processing and archiving centres that serve open data.

Slide 59

JWST: one institute is both MOC and SOC — and the DSN is shared with everyone

STScI in Baltimore is both the MOC and the SOC of JWST. For Hubble, flight operations are at NASA Goddard and science operations at STScI.

Links: S-band uplink at 16 kbit/s and downlink at 40 kbit/s for commands and engineering data; Ka-band at 25.9 GHz up to 28 Mbit/s for science. The 68 GB recorder fills in about a day, so a missed DSN contact quickly costs science; DSN windows are booked 12–20 weeks ahead; up to 57 GB/day.

Check yourself
One advantage and one risk of merging MOC and SOC?

Advantage: one team, one plan, fewer interfaces. Risk: less independent cross-checking; one organisation's priorities dominate.

Slide 60

Solar Orbiter: a changing orbit means science is planned orbit by orbit

Solar Orbiter's orbit changes a lot from one orbit to the next, so the Science Working Team and the SOC plan each science orbit in detail. ESOC receives all telemetry and archives the raw packets; the SOC at ESAC passes data to each instrument team for calibration and verification; the teams return calibrated products, which the SOC places in the ESA archive.

Timeline: cruise of about 2 to 3.5 years, a nominal science phase of about 4 years, and an extended mission of up to 10 years in total.

Slide 61

Four missions, four ground segments — the same functions in different places

All four missions have the same functions — stations, SLE, processing chain, monitoring, planning, flight dynamics, archive — organised differently: an ESA split (Gaia, Solar Orbiter), one institute for both (JWST), and an operational Earth-observation system with a separate payload data ground segment (Sentinel-2).

Trends: ground stations bought as a service, cloud processing, automation, laser relays, and common software cores.

Slide 62

Concept check

Answer each question, then open the answer to check.

1. Which centre books ground-station passes and determines the orbit?

The MOC (ground-station scheduling and flight dynamics).

2. What does the APID in a packet header identify?

The application process that produced or receives the packet; it is used for routing.

3. What stops a replayed, captured telecommand?

Authentication with a sequence number (anti-replay): the MAC is valid but the sequence number is old.

4. Level-0 data are…

Reconstructed, unprocessed instrument data at full resolution, with transmission artefacts removed.

5. Which SLE service carries commands from the MOC to the station?

F-CLTU (Forward CLTU).

Slide 63

Key takeaways

TT&C carries the data; the subject is the data. Telemetry is packets → frames → CADUs, with PUS services giving meaning. Authenticate every command; encrypt what is sensitive. Data come down in passes: real-time first, then playback; delete only after confirmed receipt.

The ground segment = stations + SLE + MOC + SOC + archives, tested like the spacecraft. On the ground: frames → packets → parameters → calibrated values → limits → alarms and archive. The MOC flies, the SOC does the science, the planning loop joins them.

PART B

Backup slides (optional reading)

Slides 66–80

Slide 66

Avionics and on-board data handling: one set of electronics, many jobs

Avionics can mean only the AOCS electronics, but usually means all platform electronics hardware and software: AOCS, TM/TC, data communications, processing, storage and the transponder.

The on-board data-handling (OBDH) functions are: data flow for housekeeping and science; receiving and distributing commands; TM/TC protocols; time distribution and datation (time-stamping from an ultra-stable oscillator and a mission epoch); data storage; executing commands and schedules; controlling payloads and subsystems; monitoring health; autonomous decisions; and data compression.

Check yourself
Why must the spacecraft distribute a common time?

All measurements must be time-stamped consistently (datation) so data from different instruments can be combined, and time-tagged commands must execute at the right moment.

Slide 67

Telemetry plays a role in every mission phase — but its job changes

During ground testing engineers have direct access to the avionics buses, so rates can be high; RF links are used for performance testing. At launch only key housekeeping is sent (battery, temperatures, reaction wheels); payloads are off. In transfer and intermediate orbits the spacecraft must be autonomous with limited contact unless relays are used. In the operational orbit the full telemetry plan applies.

Slide 68

Telemetry design starts with a telemetry list — a living document from Phase A onwards

Telemetry design starts with the telemetry list, started in the Phase A feasibility study and updated throughout. Each item has a unique identifier, a data type (analogue, digital bi-level, digital serial), a required accuracy and a sampling rate. A nutation sensor needs fast sampling; equipment temperatures slow sampling. Include spare channels for growth.

The second step is to lay out the PCM message format.

Slide 69

Redundancy is a reliability trade: a second transponder turns a 1-year design into an ~8-year designfrom [2]

Unit lifetime is modelled as exponential: P(t) = e−λt, with λ in FIT (failures per 10⁹ h). An active unit has λ = λONdON + λOFF(1 − dON).

With one active and one passive transponder, a Markov-chain analysis gives the reliability of the pair; the subsystem reliability multiplies it by the RFDN and both LGAs. With typical values the redundant subsystem stays above 99 % for about 8.5 years; a single transponder only for under a year.

PT2(t) = e−λAt[1 + (λA/λP)(1 − e−λPt)]
PTT&C(t) = PT2(t) · PRFDN(t) · PLGA(t)²
Try it in the deck: Move the failure rates, duty cycle and mission lifetime; watch the time to 99 %.
Check yourself
Convert 1500 FIT to failures per year.

1500 × 10⁻⁹ /h × 8766 h ≈ 0.0131 per year.

Why might a CubeSat fly without transponder redundancy?

Short missions accept higher risk, and redundancy costs mass, power and money.

Slide 70

How often is a TC frame rejected — or worse, accepted with errors?from [2]

A TC frame is rejected if the previous tail is missed, the start sequence is not recognised (two or more errors in 16 bits), or a codeblock is rejected. An undetected error means a corrupted frame is accepted — far worse. Typical requirements: Prej ≤ 10⁻³ and Pund ≤ 10⁻⁹, with channel BER Pb = 10⁻⁵ (ECSS). Longer CLTUs raise both; a 16-bit CRC in the frame lowers Pund by many orders of magnitude.

Pstart = 1 − (1−Pb)¹⁶ − 16Pb(1−Pb)¹⁵
Prej ≈ Ptail + (1−Ptail)[Pstart + (1−Pstart)PBCH]
Try it in the deck: Move Pb and the number of codewords until a requirement fails.
Slide 71

Autonomy: the data-handling subsystem must keep the spacecraft safe between contacts

Missions without continuous contact need autonomy and a fail-safe survival mode: decoding and reconfiguration electronics can act on TC and housekeeping directly, bypassing the central unit. Remote Terminal Units relay 16-bit commands and collect serial, bi-level and (conditioned, digitised) analogue telemetry; communications processors are intelligent terminal units that can packetize payload data.

Slide 72

Data rates decide the bus: multi-drop for control, point-to-point for blocks of data

Multi-drop buses (ESA OBDH, MIL-STD-1553B, CAN) let one master talk to many terminals at up to ~1 Mbps — commanding, telemetry, moderate science data. Point-to-point links (SpaceWire, HotLinks, GigaLink) carry blocks of data at 10 Mbps to 1 Gbps or more.

Platform sensor processing (conditioning, ADC, manipulation) runs up to ~20 Mbps; payload processing (filtering, compression, feature extraction, formatting, error control, encryption) at 200 Mbps or more.

Slide 73

AOS and Proximity-1 extended CCSDS beyond simple packet telemetry

AOS (Advanced Orbiting Systems) was created when the ISS and EO systems exceeded packet telemetry: it added isochronous (voice/video), high-volume and interactive services, a service-driven structure, and networking (path protocol and IP).

Proximity-1 serves power-constrained inter-satellite and planetary links (e.g. Mars rovers to orbiters). It is symmetric (no TM/TC distinction), with automatic link detection and negotiation, reliable in-sequence delivery by retransmission, convolutional and RS coding in both directions, and fixed- or variable-length frames.

Slide 74

The Interplanetary Internet stitches separate internets together with bundles

The Interplanetary Internet (an IRTF initiative) has four components: in-situ internets (Earth, Mars) with TCP/IP; an interplanetary backbone using CFDP techniques; gateways between them; and inter-internet dialogues that store and forward data across long delays and broken paths. These dialogues use bundling: what IP does across subnets in real time, bundling does across internets in store-and-forward fashion.

Slide 75

Payload data handling and on-board computers are converging with terrestrial practice

A PDHT (payload data handling and transmission) system handles, stores and transmits high-rate instrument data on its own RF link; tape recorders (>10 Gbit) gave way to solid-state memory. On-board computers use radiation-tolerant 32-bit processors, microcontrollers or DSPs, software written to high standards (Ada, ANSI C) and increasingly real-time operating systems. Off-the-shelf software brings faster, cheaper development, built-in file handling and multitasking, libraries, and easier maintenance.

Slide 76

A generalized instrument is a small spacecraft data system of its own

A generalized instrument chains scene → front end (optics/RF) → detection → conversion → signal processing → compression → storage → data output, with control and timing serving every block. A local controller (e.g. a SPARC-based LEON processor or a DSP) runs it in real time; output is usually in source packets, and instruments are often multimode. Examples: radar altimeters and ASAR (Envisat), microwave sounders (MHS on NOAA/MetOp), radiometers (Meteosat), hyperspectral imagers (CHRIS on PROBA), lidar (ALADIN on Aeolus), star sensors.

Slide 77

Space electronics must survive launch, vacuum, temperature — and radiation

Space electronics must save mass, power and volume and survive launch vibration, temperature extremes and vacuum; avoid pressurized voids and outgassing. Radiation has three main effects: SEU (temporary bit flips; mitigated by EDAC, scrubbing, triple-module redundancy, watchdogs), total dose (cumulative, 1–100 krad; shielding) and latch-up (destructive current; shielding or current limiting and reset). Unpowered devices are much less vulnerable.

Check yourself
Which radiation effect is cumulative and which can destroy a device instantly?

Total dose is cumulative; latch-up can be destructive.

Slide 78

Space processors lag terrestrial ones — and that is usually fine

Space processors lag terrestrial ones by years, which is usually fine for attitude control and housekeeping; simple 8-bit microcontrollers can be enough, and 32-bit processors and DSPs exist for heavier tasks. Peripherals (RAM, ROM, I/O controllers, UARTs) are the harder part to qualify and are often custom or in programmable logic. Choose bus width carefully.

Slide 79

ASICs, then rad-hard FPGAs, transformed space electronics

Electronics evolved from discrete logic (large, many PCB iterations) to ASICs (compact but costly) to radiation-hardened FPGAs (designed on a desktop, fast iteration, used to prototype ASICs, some reprogrammable), allowing single-board designs. High cost and risk demand strict requirements control and verification: VHDL, circuit simulation, auto layout and routing, standards and interface control documents.

Slide 80

Three families of standards shape every TT&C designfrom [2]

ECSS gives European projects one coherent set of standards; TT&C lives in discipline E-50. CCSDS is the inter-agency committee for space data systems (blue books = standards, green = informative, orange = experimental). SFCG coordinates frequencies where the ITU does not, e.g. for lunar and Martian links. In practice: start from ECSS E-50, go to CCSDS for new formats and protocols, and to ITU/SFCG for frequencies.
